Content:
The formula for the area of a general triangle is
[MATH: \mathcal{A}=\frac{1}{2}{\color{red}{a}}{\color{blue}{b}}\sin{C},]
where [MATH: \color{red}a] and [MATH: \color{blue}b] are two sides of the triangle and [MATH: C] is the measure of the angle between those sides (called the included angle).

Content:
We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

Content:
To demonstrate how this works, suppose that we want to calculate the area of the non-right-angled triangle below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4c41cbb9d027469659dd8ba71061c10e]

Content:
Let's call the lengths of the sides [MATH: BC = \color{red}{a}] and [MATH: AC ={\color{blue}{b}}.] For the triangle above we have
[MATH: {\color{red}a=10},] [MATH: {\color{blue}b=12},] and [MATH: m\angle C=45^{\circ}.]

Content:
Therefore, the area of our triangle is
[MATH: A|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 10 ⋅ 12 ⋅ \sin 45^{∘}; = 60 ⋅ (sqrt(2))/(2); = 30sqrt(2).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The formula for the area of the triangle is [MATH: \mathcal{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin{C},] where [MATH: \angle{C}] is between the sides of lengths [MATH: a] and [MATH: b.]

Here, we have [MATH: a|= CB = 58; b|= CA = 40; m∠C|= 31^{∘}.]

Since [MATH: \sin{31^{\circ}} = 0.515\,038] rounded to six decimal places, we calculate the area as follows: [MATH: A|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 58 ⋅ 40\sin 31^{∘}; = 1160 ⋅ (0.515038); ≈ 597.44,] rounded to two decimal places.

[IMG: /graphics/baf9217d37cc64a0caa8560240c0a729]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The formula for the area of the triangle is [MATH: \mathcal{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}bc\sin{A},] where [MATH: \angle{A}] is between the sides of lengths [MATH: b] and [MATH: c.]

Here [MATH: c|= AB,; b|= AC = 12cm,; m∠A|= 45^{∘}.]

Since [MATH: \sin{45^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2},] we can calculate [MATH: c=AB,] as follows: [MATH: A|= (1)/(2) ⋅ b ⋅ c ⋅ \sin A; 24sqrt(2)|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 12 ⋅ c ⋅ \sin 45^{∘}; 24sqrt(2)|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 12 ⋅ c ⋅ ((sqrt(2))/(2)); 24sqrt(2)|= 3sqrt(2)c; 24|= 3c; c|= 8cm.]

We conclude that [MATH: AB = 8\,\textrm{cm}.]

items.title: Calculating the Area of a Quadrilateral

sections.normalized_html: Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the area of the quadrilateral [MATH: ABCD?]
sections.readable_text:
Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the area of the quadrilateral [MATH: ABCD?]

[IMG: /graphics/df17bd0e04a4bf54f78403799e52df63]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The area of the quadrilateral [MATH: ABCD] is the sum of the areas of the triangles [MATH: \triangle ABC] and [MATH: \triangle ADC] (see the illustration below).

First, we find the area for [MATH: \triangle ABC,] and get [MATH: A_{ABC}|= (1)/(2)(42)(35)\sin 36^{∘}; = 735\sin 36^{∘}; ≈ 432.022] rounded to three decimal places.

Now we find the area for [MATH: \triangle ADC,] and get [MATH: A_{ADC}|= (1)/(2)(20)(18)\sin 80^{∘}; = 180\sin 80^{∘}; ≈ 177.265] rounded to three decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of [MATH: ABCD.] We get [MATH: A_{ABCD}|= A_{ABC} + A_{ADC}; = 432.022 + 177.265; ≈ 609]

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral [MATH: ABCD] is [MATH: 609.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the area of [MATH: \triangle ACD.] We get [MATH: A_{ACD}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ DA ⋅ DC ⋅ \sin D; = (1)/(2)(25)(32)\sin 70^{∘}; = 400\sin 70^{∘}; = 375.877...; ≈ 376cm^{2}] rounded to the nearest integer.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The formula for the area of a general triangle is
[MATH: \mathcal{A}=\frac{1}{2}{\color{red}{a}}{\color{blue}{b}}\sin{C},]
where [MATH: \color{red}a] and [MATH: \color{blue}b] are two sides of the triangle and [MATH: C] is the measure of the angle between those sides (called the included angle).

Content:
We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

Content:
To demonstrate how this works, suppose that we want to calculate the area of the non-right-angled triangle below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4c41cbb9d027469659dd8ba71061c10e]

Content:
Let's call the lengths of the sides [MATH: BC = \color{red}{a}] and [MATH: AC ={\color{blue}{b}}.] For the triangle above we have
[MATH: {\color{red}a=10},] [MATH: {\color{blue}b=12},] and [MATH: m\angle C=45^{\circ}.]

Content:
Therefore, the area of our triangle is
[MATH: A|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 10 ⋅ 12 ⋅ \sin 45^{∘}; = 60 ⋅ (sqrt(2))/(2); = 30sqrt(2).]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:

where [MATH: \angle{C}] is between the sides of lengths [MATH: a] and [MATH: b.]

Here, we have
[MATH: a|= CB = 58; b|= CA = 40; m∠C|= 31^{∘}.]

Since
[MATH: \sin{31^{\circ}} = 0.515\,038]
rounded to six decimal places, we calculate the area as follows:
[MATH: A|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 58 ⋅ 40\sin 31^{∘}; = 1160 ⋅ (0.515038); ≈ 597.44,]
rounded to two decimal places.

Item 5 — Example: Calculating an Angle or Side of a Triangle Given the Area of a Triangle

Example Prompt:
The area of ​​the triangle [MATH: \triangle ABC] is [MATH: 24\sqrt{2} \text{ cm}^2.] Find [MATH: AB.]

[IMG: /graphics/baf9217d37cc64a0caa8560240c0a729]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The formula for the area of the triangle is
[MATH: \mathcal{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}bc\sin{A},]
where [MATH: \angle{A}] is between the sides of lengths [MATH: b] and [MATH: c.]

Here
[MATH: c|= AB,; b|= AC = 12cm,; m∠A|= 45^{∘}.]

Since
[MATH: \sin{45^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2},]
we can calculate [MATH: c=AB,] as follows:
[MATH: A|= (1)/(2) ⋅ b ⋅ c ⋅ \sin A; 24sqrt(2)|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 12 ⋅ c ⋅ \sin 45^{∘}; 24sqrt(2)|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 12 ⋅ c ⋅ ((sqrt(2))/(2)); 24sqrt(2)|= 3sqrt(2)c; 24|= 3c; c|= 8cm.]

We conclude that [MATH: AB = 8\,\textrm{cm}.]

Item 8 — Example: Calculating the Area of a Quadrilateral

Example Prompt:
Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the area of the quadrilateral [MATH: ABCD?]

[IMG: /graphics/df17bd0e04a4bf54f78403799e52df63]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The area of the quadrilateral [MATH: ABCD] is the sum of the areas of the triangles [MATH: \triangle ABC] and [MATH: \triangle ADC] (see the illustration below).

[IMG: /graphics/43f655045f30483b6371dd630b70d121]

First, we find the area for [MATH: \triangle ABC,] and get
[MATH: A_{ABC}|= (1)/(2)(42)(35)\sin 36^{∘}; = 735\sin 36^{∘}; ≈ 432.022]
rounded to three decimal places.

Now we find the area for [MATH: \triangle ADC,] and get
[MATH: A_{ADC}|= (1)/(2)(20)(18)\sin 80^{∘}; = 180\sin 80^{∘}; ≈ 177.265]
rounded to three decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of [MATH: ABCD.] We get
[MATH: A_{ABCD}|= A_{ABC} + A_{ADC}; = 432.022 + 177.265; ≈ 609]

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral [MATH: ABCD] is [MATH: 609.]

Item 11 — Example: Finding the Area of a Triangle Given the Area of a Quadrilateral

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's start by finding the area of [MATH: \triangle ACD.] We get
[MATH: A_{ACD}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ DA ⋅ DC ⋅ \sin D; = (1)/(2)(25)(32)\sin 70^{∘}; = 400\sin 70^{∘}; = 375.877...; ≈ 376cm^{2}]
rounded to the nearest integer.

The difference of the areas of the quadrilateral [MATH: ABCD] and [MATH: \triangle ACD] gives the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC.] Therefore,
[MATH: A_{ABC}|= A_{ACD} − A_{ABCD}; = 376 − 300; = 76cm^{2}.]

Item 14 — Tutorial: Deriving the Formula for the Area of a General Triangle

Content:
Consider [MATH: \triangle ABC] with sides of lengths [MATH: a,b,] and [MATH: c,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/85cb06d9cd067b372393114bddfa976d]

Content:
Let's now add the height of length [MATH: h] perpendicular to [MATH: \overline{BC},] as shown.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5b6c83c07b7266920d24646cfb6f22af]

Content:
Using the usual formula for the area [MATH: \mathcal A] of a triangle in terms of its base and height, we have

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal A = \dfrac12 ah.]

Content:
Using elementary trigonometry, we have that

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{h}{b} = \sin C]
which means that

Content:
[MATH: h = b\sin C.]

Content:
Therefore, by substituting this into our expression for [MATH: \mathcal A,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal A = \dfrac12ab\sin C]
as required.

Content:
We can use a similar approach to prove the following formulas:

Content:
[MATH: A|= (1)/(2)bc\sin A; A|= (1)/(2)ac\sin B]
